note: 50 questions, all one level. Built for surprise while staying guessable. Every citation points at a source retrieved during research.

questions.prompt: About how many people in the world face hunger?
questions.whyCorrect: About 1 in 12 people — 8.2% of everyone alive — faced hunger in 2024. In a school of 600, that's 50 people.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic — the real rate is roughly eight times higher.
Nowhere near. Hunger affects hundreds of millions of people.
questions.action: Work out 1 in 12 of your school's population.

questions.prompt: How many people can't reliably get enough safe, nutritious food?
questions.whyCorrect: 2.3 billion people — 28% of the world — were moderately or severely food insecure in 2024. That's more than one in four of us.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
A hundred times too low.
questions.action: Notice the difference between 'hungry today' and 'never sure there'll be enough'.

questions.prompt: Compared with 2015, how many MORE people are food insecure today?
questions.whyCorrect: 683 million more than in 2015. Unlike extreme poverty, which fell for decades, food insecurity has been getting worse.
whyWrong: It rose sharply — from 1.6 billion in 2015 to 2.3 billion.
This is one of the SDGs moving backwards, not forwards.
questions.action: Ask what changed after 2015 — think conflict, COVID, climate and prices.

questions.prompt: What share of children under 5 are stunted — permanently shorter and often slower to develop because of poor nutrition?
questions.whyCorrect: 23.2% — nearly one in four children worldwide. Stunting happens in the first 1,000 days of life and can never be fully reversed.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
Too high — though the real number is bad enough.
questions.action: Look up what the 'first 1,000 days' means for a child's growth.

questions.prompt: Child stunting is falling. But which form of child malnutrition is RISING?
questions.whyCorrect: Child overweight rose from 5.3% to 5.5%. Many countries now face hunger and obesity at the same time — often in the same neighbourhoods.
whyWrong: Stunting fell from 26.4% to 23.2%.
Wasting fell from 7.4% to 6.6%.
questions.action: Ask how a country can have hungry and overweight children at once.

questions.prompt: Anaemia — dangerous iron deficiency — affects what share of women aged 15 to 49?
questions.whyCorrect: 30.7% of women — nearly one in three. And it's getting worse, up from 27.6% in 2012.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
Too high, though the real figure is alarming enough.
questions.action: Look up which foods are richest in iron.

questions.prompt: Among children aged 6 to 23 months, what share eat a varied enough diet to grow properly?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 34% — about one in three. Two-thirds of the world's babies aren't getting the variety of food their brains and bodies need.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic.
Nowhere near — most young children don't meet this standard.
questions.action: Count how many different foods you ate yesterday.

questions.prompt: Which region has the highest share of undernourished people?
questions.whyCorrect: Sub-Saharan Africa, at 22.3% — more than one in five people. Northern Africa and Western Asia is next at 11.8%.
whyWrong: Europe has food insecurity, but nothing on this scale.
High at 11.8%, but roughly half the Sub-Saharan rate.
questions.action: Find Sub-Saharan Africa on a map.

questions.prompt: In 2022, what share of countries were hit by unusually high food prices?
questions.whyCorrect: 60% of all countries — up from just 16% in 2015. When food prices spike, the poorest families feel it first because food is most of what they buy.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
Not every country, though the majority were affected.
questions.action: Ask an adult whether food got more expensive recently.

questions.prompt: Food prices fell sharply for most countries in 2024. Who was left behind?
questions.whyCorrect: Globally the share of countries with high food prices dropped to 15.3%, but 31.6% of least developed countries were still paying elevated prices — double the global rate.
whyWrong: Wealthy countries absorb price shocks most easily.
The recovery was very uneven.
questions.action: Ask why a global price drop might not reach everyone.

questions.prompt: How many people are projected to still face hunger in 2030 — the year hunger was meant to end?
questions.whyCorrect: Over 600 million people. The goal is called Zero Hunger, and on the current path the world will miss it by hundreds of millions.
whyWrong: That's the target, but not the projection.
The projection is more than a hundred times higher.
questions.action: Name one thing that would change that projection.

questions.prompt: How much do governments worldwide spend on agriculture each year?
questions.whyCorrect: About $701 billion a year. Enormous — the question is whether it reaches small farmers and nutritious crops, or mostly large producers.
whyWrong: A thousand times too low.
A hundred times too low.
questions.action: Ask who benefits most from farm spending in your country.

questions.prompt: Aid for agriculture in developing countries has changed since 2015. Which way?
questions.whyCorrect: It rose from $12.9 billion to $18.5 billion. Genuine progress — even while hunger itself got worse.
whyWrong: It grew by more than 40%.
It moved upwards, not down.
questions.action: Ask why more money can go in while outcomes still worsen.

questions.prompt: Global hunger has been slowly improving. From 8.7% in 2022, where is it now?
questions.whyCorrect: 8.2% in 2024, down from 8.7% in 2022 and 8.5% in 2023. Slow improvement — but still far above where the world was before 2020.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic — that would be near the goal.
Hunger has been easing slightly, not rising to this level.
questions.action: Notice that 0.5 percentage points is still tens of millions of people.

questions.prompt: What share of women worldwide eat a diverse enough diet to be healthy?
questions.whyCorrect: 65% — meaning about a third of women don't get the variety of nutrients they need, even when they get enough calories.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic, though the real gap is serious.
Too optimistic — a third of women fall short.
questions.action: Notice the difference between 'enough food' and 'the right food'.

questions.prompt: Anaemia is worst among which group of women?
questions.whyCorrect: 35.5% of pregnant women are anaemic — higher than the 30.5% rate for non-pregnant women. Pregnancy raises iron needs sharply.
whyWrong: The measured group is women aged 15 to 49.
It affects women across that whole age range, not just teenagers.
questions.action: Ask why pregnancy increases the body's need for iron.

questions.prompt: Child wasting means a child is dangerously thin for their height. What share of under-5s does it affect?
questions.whyCorrect: 6.6% — about 1 in 15 young children. Wasting is the most immediately life-threatening form of malnutrition.
whyWrong: That's closer to the stunting figure of 23.2%.
Ten times too low.
questions.action: Look up the difference between stunting and wasting.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many people faced hunger in 2024?
questions.whyCorrect: Between 638 and 720 million people. Estimates give a range because measuring hunger in war zones and remote areas is genuinely hard.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
A hundred times too low.
questions.action: Ask why hunger figures are given as a range.

questions.prompt: In 2015, how many people were food insecure?
questions.whyCorrect: 1.6 billion, or 21.4% of the world. By 2024 that had grown to 2.3 billion and 28%.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
Too high for 2015 — though the trend is heading that way.
questions.action: Compare 21.4% in 2015 with 28% today.

questions.prompt: Since 2012, child stunting has moved which way?
questions.whyCorrect: Down from 26.4% to 23.2%. Millions of children are growing up healthier than they would have a decade ago.
whyWrong: It improved rather than worsened.
It fell by over 3 percentage points.
questions.action: Notice which hunger numbers improved and which got worse.

questions.prompt: Which statement is true about the world's food?
options: There isn't enough food for everyone
Food shortages are only caused by drought
There's enough food, but not everyone can get or afford it
questions.whyCorrect: The world produces enough food. Hunger is driven by poverty, conflict, prices and distribution — 2.3 billion people can't reliably access what already exists.
whyWrong: Global production is sufficient; access is the problem.
Drought matters, but conflict, prices and poverty drive most hunger.
questions.action: Ask what stops food reaching people who need it.

questions.prompt: One in four children worldwide is stunted. What causes it?
options: Poor nutrition in the first years of life
questions.whyCorrect: Chronic poor nutrition, especially in the first 1,000 days. The damage to height and brain development is largely permanent.
whyWrong: Stunting is about nutrition, not activity levels.
Screen time has nothing to do with stunted growth.
questions.action: Look up what nutrients a growing child needs most.

questions.prompt: Since 2012, anaemia in women has gone which way?
questions.whyCorrect: Worse — up from 27.6% to 30.7%. It's one of the clearest signs that diet quality, not just quantity, is slipping.
whyWrong: It moved in the wrong direction.
It rose by about 3 percentage points.
questions.action: Ask why a health measure might worsen while hunger falls.

questions.prompt: In 2015 only 16% of countries had high food prices. What happened by 2022?
questions.whyCorrect: It jumped to 60% of all countries — nearly a fourfold increase driven by the pandemic, conflict and supply disruption.
whyWrong: Prices rose sharply rather than falling.
It nearly quadrupled.
questions.action: Ask what happened between 2015 and 2022 to push food prices up.

questions.prompt: Zero Hunger is Goal 2. What year was it meant to be achieved by?
questions.whyCorrect: 2030 — the deadline for all 17 Goals. With 600 million people projected to still be hungry, this one will be missed.
whyWrong: That's a common target year for climate goals, not the SDGs.
The SDGs run to 2030, not the end of the century.
questions.action: Work out how old you'll be in 2030.

questions.prompt: Which is more common worldwide: children who are stunted, or children who are overweight?
questions.whyCorrect: 23.2% stunted against 5.5% overweight — roughly four times as many. Both are forms of malnutrition, and both are rising in some countries.
whyWrong: There's a large gap between them.
Stunting is about four times more common.
questions.action: Ask how one country can have both problems at once.

questions.prompt: Food insecurity means what, exactly?
options: Only eating one meal a day
Not being able to reliably get enough safe, nutritious food
questions.whyCorrect: It means not being able to count on getting enough safe, nutritious food. It runs from worrying about running out, all the way to going days without eating.
whyWrong: That's one severe form, but food insecurity covers a wider range.
Preference isn't the measure — reliable access is.
questions.action: Notice that food insecurity is a spectrum, not one thing.

questions.prompt: About what share of the world is moderately or severely food insecure?
questions.whyCorrect: 28% — well over a quarter of everyone alive. That's a much bigger group than the 8.2% who face outright hunger.
whyWrong: That's the hunger figure. Food insecurity is a wider measure.
Too high, though the real number is more than one in four.
questions.action: Compare 8.2% hungry with 28% food insecure. What's the difference?

questions.prompt: Least developed countries face high food prices at what rate compared to their own historical average?
questions.whyCorrect: 31.6% against a historical average of 18% — nearly double. The countries least able to absorb price shocks are getting hit hardest and longest.
whyWrong: They're above their historical average, not below.
There's a substantial gap.
questions.action: Ask what a family does when food prices double.

questions.prompt: How many children under 5 are affected by stunting or wasting or being overweight?
questions.whyCorrect: Adding 23.2% stunted, 6.6% wasted and 5.5% overweight gets you to around a third of all young children affected by some form of malnutrition.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic.
Nowhere near — malnutrition affects hundreds of millions of children.
questions.action: Add the three percentages yourself and see.

questions.prompt: Hunger fell for decades and then reversed. Roughly when did it turn?
questions.whyCorrect: Around 2015, food insecurity started climbing — from 1.6 billion people then to 2.3 billion now. Conflict, COVID and price shocks all stacked up.
whyWrong: 683 million more people are food insecure than in 2015.
The 1990s and 2000s saw steady improvement.
questions.action: Ask what makes progress reverse after decades of gains.

questions.prompt: In low-income countries, is child malnutrition mainly a problem of too little food or poor-quality food?
questions.whyCorrect: Both. Only 34% of young children get a varied enough diet, and 23.2% are stunted — you need enough food and the right nutrients in it.
whyWrong: Sheer quantity matters too, especially in famine and conflict.
Diet variety matters enormously — a child fed only rice still becomes malnourished.
questions.action: Plan a day of meals that has both enough food and enough variety.

questions.prompt: Northern Africa and Western Asia has an undernourishment rate of about:
questions.whyCorrect: 11.8% — roughly one in eight people, and above the global average of 8.2%.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
Too high — that's beyond even Sub-Saharan Africa's 22.3%.
questions.action: Compare that with the global 8.2% and Sub-Saharan Africa's 22.3%.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a real measure of child hunger used worldwide?
questions.whyCorrect: Height for age is exactly how stunting is measured — a child too short for their age has been chronically undernourished.
whyWrong: Not a nutrition measure.
Not used to measure malnutrition.
questions.action: Look up a child growth chart and see how it works.

questions.prompt: Global spending on agriculture is $701 billion a year. Aid for agriculture is:
questions.whyCorrect: $18.5 billion — under 3% of what governments spend on their own agriculture. Most farm money is domestic, not aid.
whyWrong: Aid is a small fraction of total agricultural spending.
That would be nearly all of it.
questions.action: Work out what share $18.5bn is of $701bn.

questions.prompt: 'Hunger' and 'food insecurity' — which affects more people?
options: Food insecurity, by about three times
questions.whyCorrect: 2.3 billion food insecure against roughly 700 million hungry. Food insecurity catches everyone who can't count on their next meal, not just those going without today.
whyWrong: It's the other way round — food insecurity is the wider category.
They measure different things and differ by over a billion people.
questions.action: Explain the difference to someone in one sentence.

questions.prompt: Child overweight rates are rising. What does that suggest about the world's food system?
options: Children are eating too many vegetables
Cheap, low-nutrition food is often the most available
Food has become too expensive everywhere
questions.whyCorrect: When the cheapest, easiest food is high in sugar and fat and low in nutrients, families can be overweight and undernourished at the same time.
whyWrong: Only 34% of young children get enough dietary variety.
Prices fell in most countries in 2024, yet overweight rates kept rising.
questions.action: Compare the price of fresh vegetables and crisps where you shop.

questions.prompt: Since 2012, child wasting has moved which way?
questions.whyCorrect: Down from 7.4% to 6.6%. Slow but real progress on the most immediately dangerous form of child malnutrition.
whyWrong: It fell by nearly one percentage point.
It improved rather than worsened.
questions.action: Notice that small percentage falls mean millions of children.

questions.prompt: If 28% of the world is food insecure, roughly how many people is that?
questions.whyCorrect: 2.3 billion people. Percentages hide scale — always convert them back into human beings.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
More than the world's population.
questions.action: Next percentage you read, turn it into a number of people.

questions.prompt: The world set targets on child stunting and wasting for which year?
questions.whyCorrect: 2025 — and the UN says a fundamental shift is needed even to meet the wider 2030 nutrition goals.
whyWrong: Far beyond any SDG deadline.
The nutrition targets came far earlier than this.
questions.action: Ask what happens when a target year passes unmet.

questions.prompt: Which is the better description of hunger's main cause?
options: Mostly people choosing not to farm
questions.whyCorrect: Hunger tracks poverty, war and food prices far more closely than weather alone. Food insecurity rose 683 million since 2015 largely from conflict, COVID and price shocks.
whyWrong: Weather matters, but it isn't the main driver.
Hundreds of millions of people farm and are still hungry.
questions.action: Name the three biggest drivers of hunger in your own words.

questions.prompt: Roughly one in three young children misses out on a varied diet. What's the risk?
options: Their brains and bodies don't develop fully
questions.whyCorrect: Without variety a child can get enough calories and still lack the iron, vitamins and protein their brain and body need — which is how stunting happens.
whyWrong: Poor nutrition stunts growth rather than boosting it.
Variety is exactly what the dietary diversity measure tracks.
questions.action: List five different food groups you ate this week.

questions.prompt: Which country group is most exposed when global food prices spike?
questions.whyCorrect: Least developed countries — 31.6% still faced high prices in 2024 while the global figure fell to 15.3%. Poorer households spend most of their income on food.
whyWrong: Wealthy countries absorb shocks most easily.
The impact is deeply unequal.
questions.action: Work out what share of your household budget goes on food.

questions.prompt: Global undernourishment in 2023 was:
questions.whyCorrect: 8.5% — between 8.7% in 2022 and 8.2% in 2024, showing slow year-on-year improvement.
whyWrong: Too high — that's more than double the real figure.
Ten times too low.
questions.action: Chart 8.7, 8.5, 8.2 and see the direction.

questions.prompt: Why is hunger described as a solvable problem?
options: Because hunger is not really measured
The world grows enough food already
questions.whyCorrect: Enough food exists; the failures are in poverty, conflict, prices and distribution. That makes hunger a political and economic problem, not a physical impossibility.
whyWrong: It's measured extensively through household surveys worldwide.
2.3 billion people are food insecure.
questions.action: Ask what would have to change for food to reach everyone.

questions.prompt: About how many children under 5 are stunted, wasted or overweight — put another way?
questions.whyCorrect: Hundreds of millions. With roughly a third of all under-5s affected, malnutrition is one of the largest health problems on Earth.
whyWrong: Vastly too low.
Still hundreds of times too low.
questions.action: Look up how many children under 5 there are in the world.

questions.prompt: Which has improved since 2012 — stunting, or anaemia in women?
questions.whyCorrect: Stunting fell from 26.4% to 23.2%, while anaemia rose from 27.6% to 30.7%. Progress on nutrition is genuinely mixed.
whyWrong: It's the reverse of this.
Anaemia moved in the wrong direction.
questions.action: Ask why one nutrition measure can improve while another worsens.

questions.prompt: If 1 in 12 people face hunger, how many is that in a city of 120,000?
questions.whyCorrect: About 10,000 people — one in twelve. Scaling global percentages to somewhere you know makes them real.
whyWrong: That would be 1 in 120.
That would be 1 in 1,200.
questions.action: Work out the figure for your own town.

questions.prompt: The share of countries with high food prices went from 60% in 2022 to what in 2024?
questions.whyCorrect: 15.3% — a dramatic improvement in two years. But least developed countries stayed stuck at 31.6%.
whyWrong: The fall was much steeper than this.
Prices eased substantially rather than worsening.
questions.action: Ask who benefits first when prices fall, and who benefits last.

questions.prompt: What would 'Zero Hunger' actually require?
options: Fixing poverty, conflict, prices and distribution together
Waiting for the problem to fade
questions.whyCorrect: The world already grows enough. Ending hunger means tackling why 2.3 billion people can't reliably reach it — poverty, war, price shocks and broken distribution at once.
whyWrong: Production isn't the binding constraint; access is.
Food insecurity has grown by 683 million people since 2015.
questions.action: Pick the one you'd tackle first and say why.
